text.p: Just one year after losing its men and its money in a PLO-Israeli crackdown, Hamas has bombed its way back into the Middle East political arena.

The Islamic fundamentalist group has seized on the crisis between Israel and the PLO over Jewish settlement in Jerusalem to show it is still a force, Palestinian political analysts and Hamas members said.
The movement, which condemns Yasser Arafat's self-rule deal with Israel as a sellout, is still weak and riven by strategy differences, the analysts said.
But it sees in the bulldozers that broke ground on a Jewish settlement this week the opening of a new path to popularity among frustrated and impoverished Palestinians.
An anonymous caller to Israeli police said Hamas claimed responsibility for the suicide bombing of a Tel Aviv cafe on Friday that killed three Israelis.

Israel's right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed as "immoral" a suggestion that his decision to build a settlement on the southeast Jerusalem hill of Jabal Abu Ghneim -- Har Homa in Hebrew -- had provoked the attack. He accused Arafat's Palestinian Authority (PA) of encouraging the violence by releasing Hamas prisoners.

Hamas activists say Netanyahu is wrong on both counts. They believe Netanyahu's determination to tighten his grip on Jerusalem in the face of world criticism is a humiliation for the Palestinian Authority.
"Hamas's conviction is that the peace process is not leading to any results but to more land confiscation," said one Hamas member.
"The fatal crisis experienced by the peace proces affirms Hamas's vision from the beginning," said a Hamas political leader, Sayyid Abu Musameh.
Palestinian analysts believe Netanyahu has played into the hands of peace process opponents who found a ready ear on the streets last week.
"Jabal Abu Ghneim opened the door for extremist forces to regain their positions which they had lost over the past two years," said one analyst identified with the PLO.

Hamas and the smaller Islamic Jihad tried to undermine the Oslo self-rule deals through a bombing campaign which culiminated one year ago in four suicide attacks that killed 59 people in Israel. Israel's Labour government leaned on Arafat to roll up Hamas, although it still lost power to Netanyahu in an election that turned on security.
Arafat rounded up hundreds of Hamas members, and attacked the organisation's powerbase -- its mosques, schools, charities and social welfare institutions.
"The Palestinian crackdown was harder than the (Israeli) occupation," said a source close to Hamas's military wing, Izz el-Deen al-Qassam.
"But we have been rebuilding and we have all the men and necessary things," the source said without elaborating.
Analysts said Hamas was trying to ride a wave of popular frustration with the peace process while avoiding openly challenging or embarrassing Arafat.

Most of its members have been released from PLO jails and its political and social infrastructure is beginning to be rebuilt. Accurate information about the strength and strategy of Qassam is difficult to garner.
But sources close to the group said it had demonstrated that it could not be written off.
They said the Tel Aviv bombing was planned quickly to exploit an opportunity.
They denied Netanyahu's claim that it was linked to Arafat's release a week ago of Hamas leader Ibrahim al-Makadmeh.

Political analysts doubted whether Hamas could mount a sustained bombing campaign, noting that it did not have the military or political resources to do so. But Hamas sources said Qassam could strike again if Israel targetted one of its members or if Palestinian anger continued to mount.
Makadmeh, himself, left little doubt about the future.

"We must have the control and the power to stop the bulldozers of the enemy -- and our unarmed people will not prevent it but the holy warriors carrying explosives on their shoulders and exploding the enemies of God," he told a rally in the Gaza Strip on Friday.
